blocks.text: Macroscopic collisions are generally inelastic and do not conserve kinetic energy. The perfectly inelastic collision is one in which the colliding objects stick together to make a single mass after the collision. Take two rigid bodies of masses m1 and m2 moving with velocities v1i and v2i in the two-dimensional xy-plane; the first body moves along the x-axis while the second moves in a direction making an angle theta with the x-axis, and both collide at the origin (Fig. 2.17). After the collision the bodies stick together, with combined mass M = m1 + m2, moving with velocity vf at an angle phi with the x-axis. Resolve v2i into rectangular components v2i sin theta and v2i cos theta, and vf into vf sin phi and vf cos phi.

blocks.alt: Axes x and y. Body m1 moves along the x-axis towards the origin with velocity v1i; body m2 moves towards the origin with velocity v2i along a line at angle theta to the x-axis. After colliding at the origin the combined body moves off with velocity vf at angle phi above the x-axis.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.17: Perfectly inelastic collision in two dimensions (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.17).

blocks.title: Momentum in the x- and y-directions
blocks.text: x: m1 v1i cos theta1 + m2 v2i cos theta2 = M vf cos phi ... (2.39). y: m1 v1i sin theta1 + m2 v2i sin theta2 = M vf sin phi ... (2.40).
Solving for the final velocity and angle

Magnitude of the final velocity vf: squaring and adding (2.39) and (2.40), vf = sqrt( [(m1 v1i cos theta1 + m2 v2i cos theta2)/M]^2 + [(m1 v1i sin theta1 + m2 v2i sin theta2)/M]^2 ) ... (2.41). Final angle phi: dividing the equations (2.40) by (2.41), phi = tan^-1 [ (m1 v1i sin theta1 + m2 v2i sin theta2) / (m1 v1i cos theta1 + m2 v2i cos theta2) ] ... (2.42). Here phi is the direction, with the x-axis, of the common velocity of the two bodies that stick together after the inelastic collision. Substituting the values of m1, m2, M, theta1, theta2, phi, v1i, v2i and vf in (2.39) and (2.40), the law of conservation of momentum in this case can be proved.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The angle phi comes from dividing Eq. (2.40) by Eq. (2.39) (the y-momentum equation by the x-momentum equation), not by (2.41).

Since the collision is inelastic, the kinetic energy of the colliding system is not conserved; the loss is computed as follows. The total initial kinetic energy before the collision is (KE)i = (1/2) m1 v1i^2 + (1/2) m2 v2i^2 ... (2.43); since kinetic energy is a scalar, the velocities in the formula need not be broken into components. The total final kinetic energy after the collision, when the objects stick together, is (KE)f = (1/2) M vf^2 ... (2.44), where vf is the magnitude of the final velocity from (2.41). Energy loss: since the collision is inelastic there is a loss of kinetic energy, delta KE = (KE)i - (KE)f, transformed into other forms such as heat, sound or deformation. Using m1, m2, M, v1i^2, v2i^2 and vf^2 in (2.43) and (2.44), the kinetic energy before and after an inelastic collision and the amount of energy lost can be determined.
Some examples of an inelastic collision

items: When a karate chop breaks a pile of bricks: the objects do not bounce back after impact; some of the energy of the strike is absorbed by the bricks, turning into heat, sound and the force needed to break them, so the energy goes into breaking the bricks rather than causing the hand to rebound. If the chop is not perfectly vertical and involves some horizontal motion, the momentum transfer and the resulting forces have both horizontal and vertical components.

In a car crash the collision is inelastic in both the horizontal and vertical directions: the vehicles collide and absorb the impact energy, crumpling and deforming; this energy absorption slows the cars down and stops them bouncing back, and most of the kinetic energy is lost as heat, sound and damage to the vehicles.

A ball and bat show inelastic behaviour: when the bat hits the ball some kinetic energy is lost because the ball deforms, and energy is converted into heat and sound; even though the bat is rigid it does not transfer energy perfectly and absorbs some energy itself; the ball compresses on impact, leading to further loss, so not all the initial kinetic energy is conserved and the collision is overall inelastic.
